units.spoken: SARSA: Learning the Value of the Moves You Play
Judge each step by what you will really do next, and learn a safer path.

A robot learning a floor finds the shortest path along a dangerous edge, but while it still tries random steps it keeps falling off. Can it learn a path that stays safe while it is still trying things?

Here a warehouse robot must reach its charging dock. It starts in one bottom corner and the dock sits in the other. The floor is a grid of cells. A cell, also called a square, is one position on the floor, and the state is which cell the robot stands in. It knows only which cell it stands in, not where each step leads or what it costs. The agent is the learner that picks the moves, as taught in RL Basics. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad, as taught in RL Basics.

Take a look at this figure. The floor is a grid, start at one end and dock at the other, with a narrow ledge between them. The shortest path hugs the ledge, one square from a fall. That closeness is the whole problem: the route that looks cheapest on the map is the one that costs the most while the robot is still learning, because every random step can send it back to the start.

The table carries a row per square, while only 37 squares are ever occupied: the ten red ledge squares are never occupied, since stepping onto one sends the robot back to the start, and the dock square is never occupied either, since the episode ends on entry. 48 squares minus 10 ledge squares minus the dock square leaves 37. Take the start square in Figure 1: the robot can step up to safety, but a step right onto the ledge is a fall.

An episode is one run from the start until it ends, as taught in RL Basics. The ledge is the strip of floor between the start and the dock. Sutton and Barto's textbook calls the ledge a cliff and the dock the goal. Reaching the dock can take many moves.

Each move's reward is minus the battery it uses, so the best total is the one closest to zero. Every move costs a little battery; stepping onto the ledge costs a lot and puts the robot back at the start; only reaching the dock ends the episode. The cheapest way to the dock is the shortest path that never steps onto the ledge.

sections.section: 1 Why the edge route keeps falling

units.spoken: Section one, Why the edge route keeps falling
Aim at the move you will really play
Picture the robot one square above the ledge: the shortest way to the dock runs along the edge, one wrong step from a fall.
Judge each step by the move the robot will really play next, wrong steps included, instead of the best move it could play.
When it works, the robot learns a safe route while it still explores, because the fall risk sits inside its scores.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less, as taught in RL Basics. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance, as taught in RL Basics. A move's value, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes a move in a state and plays on from there, as taught in RL Basics. If the robot never slipped, the edge route would be the cheapest way to the dock, because it is the shortest.

A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move, as taught in Q-Learning. Epsilon-greedy usually plays the top-scored move and, with chance epsilon, a random one instead, as taught in RL Basics. The discount sets how much a reward one step later still counts, as taught in RL Basics.

Q-learning's target is the step's reward plus the discounted best score in the next state, the top score there, also called the max, as taught in Q-Learning. Beside the ledge, one wrong step costs far more than any ordinary step. SARSA, named for the state, action, reward, state and action each update looks at, builds its target from the move the robot will really play, slips included, instead of the top-scored move.
One point one, The name spells the method

What this figure is teaching is that the name spells the method. Five letters, one for each thing the robot meets in a single update: the cell it stands in, the move it plays, the reward it gets, the cell it lands in, and the next move. The last letter carries the whole idea: the next move is picked before the score is updated, so the score aims at the move the robot will really play, not the best move it could play.

Read the name in Figure 2 as the order of one update: state, move, reward, next state, next move, with the last one chosen before the update. Take one step above the ledge: the robot stands in a cell, steps right, pays a little battery, lands in the next cell, and the next move it draws is down.
The table says the edge route is best, yet the episodes the robot actually runs keep losing battery to falls.
One point two, The edge route

Here is the point of this figure. The edge route is the shortest way home, and every step along it is safe. The danger is not the route itself but the exploring: one random step toward the ledge, and the robot is back at the start. That is why the edge route costs more than its length promises, and why a learner that scores the moves it really plays backs away from it.
The shortest way in Figure 3 is the trap: every step right is safe, but one random step down sends the robot back to the start. That is why the edge route costs more than its length promises.

sections.section: 2 Counting the slip into the score

units.spoken: Section two, Counting the slip into the score
The slip lives inside the score
Picture the next cell: the robot has already drawn its next move by chance, and the score it aims at is that move's score, not the best one there.
Take the score of the drawn move, even when it steps toward the ledge, and build the target from it.
When it works, the scores beside the ledge sink with the fall risk, so the robot backs off the edge on its own.

Take a look at this figure. One cell, one row of bars, and two ways to read it. Q-learning reads the tallest bar, the best move in that cell. SARSA reads the bar its drawn move points to, whichever bar that is, even the short one toward the ledge. The bars are the same; only the bar read changes. That one choice, which bar the target comes from, is the whole difference between the two methods.

Figure 4 holds the whole difference in one bar: Q-learning reads the top bar, the best move there, while SARSA reads the bar of the move it drew. Take the next cell above the ledge: the top bar runs right along the edge, but the drawn move steps down, so SARSA's target carries the fall.

sections.section: 3 Scoring the move you will play

units.spoken: Section three, Scoring the move you will play
Move a little, not all the way
Picture the played entry: it moves a little toward its target, never all the way at once.
Measure the surprise, the gap between the target and the played score, and move the played score by a share of it.
When it works, the played score creeps toward its target step by step, and only the played entry changes.

The TD (temporal difference) error is how much one step surprised the agent, the target minus the current guess, as taught in RL Basics. The guess is the played score, the table's score for the move the robot just played. The learning rate sets how big a step each update takes, as taught in RL Basics. A fall sends the robot back to the start, so it must walk the whole floor again.
The sign means drawn at random from, as taught in RL Basics. The robot stands a cell from the ledge and has already drawn its next move, which could be a slip toward the edge.
Equation 1. The robot beside the ledge does not always play its best move: with a small chance it slips, and a slip toward the ledge is a fall.
Take a look at this equation. It scores the move the robot will really play, slips included.

The drawn move line. A sub t plus one is the next move, already drawn. Pi sub epsilon is the epsilon-greedy policy that draws the moves. Usually it plays the top-scored move, and with chance epsilon it plays a random one instead. S sub t plus one is the cell the robot lands in. The sign means drawn at random from, so the move comes by chance. The dot is the slot for the drawn move, and the policy gives every move a chance. The bar means in the next cell, where the move is played. Intuitively, the next move is drawn, not guessed.
Intuition. SARSA never guesses the next move. It draws the move the robot will really play, slips included, and aims the score at that move.
Example. Take the robot in the cell just above the ledge. Epsilon-greedy draws down, the step toward the ledge, instead of the top-scored move along the edge.

The target line. Y sub t is the target for this step, one number. R sub t plus one is the step's reward for this move. Gamma is the discount, the number that shrinks a later reward. Here it is one, so the next score counts in full. Q of the next cell and the drawn move is its score. It reads the drawn move's score, not the top score there. Intuitively, the target is what this step was worth.
termList: Q of the next cell and the drawn move

units.spoken: Intuition. The target is what this step was worth: its reward plus the score of the move the robot really draws next.
Example. Take the step into the cell just above the ledge, where the drawn move is down. The target adds the step's reward to the score of that move down, so the fall risk sits inside it.

The surprise line. Delta sub t is the surprise, the gap between target and guess. Q of state s sub t and action a sub t is the played score. The minus reads as a gap, target minus guess. A positive gap means the step beat the guess, so the score rises. A negative gap means the step fell short, so the score drops. A zero gap means the guess was right, so nothing moves. Intuitively, the surprise says how far the played score missed.
termList: Q of state s sub t and action a sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. The surprise is the gap between the target and the guess. It says how far the played score missed, and in which direction.
Example. Take a step whose target sits above the played score. The gap is positive, so the played score rises.

The nudge line. Eta is the learning rate, the size of each nudge. Here it is one half, so the entry moves half the gap. The arrow reads replace with: the played score is replaced by itself plus eta times the surprise. Intuitively, the guess moves a little toward its target, never all the way.
Intuition. The guess moves a little toward its target, never all the way at once. Only the played entry changes.

Example. Take the step toward the dock where the target sits above the played score. The entry moves toward it, and the next time the robot stands in that cell, the table already holds the higher score.
Together the four lines say one thing: draw the next move first, aim the played score at it, measure the surprise, and nudge the played score toward its target.

sections.section: 4 A step near the ledge, walked stage by stage

units.spoken: Section four, A step near the ledge, walked stage by stage

What this figure is teaching is that one step, watched closely, is the whole update. A longer bar reads as more battery still to spend, and the played bar is the one that moves. Watch the token: it marks the move already drawn, and each stage follows that one move, from the draw, to the target, to the gap, to the nudge. The walk is the equation, played out one stage at a time.

Try stepping through the walk with the Next button. Watch the token on the bar: it marks the move already drawn, and each stage follows that one move. First the draw, then the target marker forms, then the gap shades in, then the played bar moves part of the way toward the marker.
One real step beside the ledge, walked one stage at a time, becomes one small change in the played score. The marker is the target, shown as a green line in the target column.
Take a look at this walk. It follows one real step through the four lines.
First stage, the drawn move. The next move is already drawn, and the token marks it.
Intuition. Every stage of the walk starts with the move already drawn. The token on the bar marks which move the walk follows.
Example. Take the walk's first stage: the robot stands a cell from the ledge, its move already chosen, and the token marks that move.
Second stage, the target. The marker forms from the step's reward plus the drawn move's score.
termList: Q of the next cell and the drawn move

units.spoken: Intuition. The walk moves on to what the landing is worth. The target adds the step's reward to the score of the drawn move.
Example. Take the walk's target stage: the marker forms from the step's reward plus the score of the token's bar, while the top bar stays outlined faintly.
Third stage, the surprise. The gap between the played bar and the target shades in.
termList: Q of state s sub t and action a sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. The walk now measures the gap between the target and the guess. That gap is the surprise this step carried.
Example. Take the walk's gap stage: the gap between the played bar and the target shades as the TD error.
Fourth stage, the nudge. The played bar moves part of the way to the marker.
Intuition. The walk ends by nudging the played score toward its target. Then the drawn move becomes the move played next.
Example. Take the walk's last stage: the played bar moves part of the way to the marker, and the token becomes the move for the next step.
Together the four stages say one thing: the drawn move sets the target, the target sets the surprise, and the surprise nudges the played score.
Figure 5 hangs this square's row of bars down, so a longer bar reads as more battery still to spend.
Section five, Whose moves teach each learner
Learn from your own moves
Picture two learners: the on-policy one learns only from its own moves, while the off-policy one also learns from moves another policy took.
How. SARSA aims its target at the drawn move, the move its own policy plays, while Q-learning aims at the top-scored move.
When it works, SARSA's scores count the slips its own exploring really makes, so its route backs off the ledge.

The greedy policy plays the top-scored move in each state, as taught in Q-Learning. The behaviour policy is the policy that picks the moves the robot plays. Q-learning's robot plays epsilon-greedy, yet its target reads the top score, the score of the move only the greedy policy would play. Near the ledge, those random moves are the ones that end in a fall.

The target policy is the policy whose score the target reads: SARSA's is the epsilon-greedy policy it plays, and Q-learning's is the greedy policy. It is a policy, a rule for choosing moves, while the target is one number, the value the played score moves toward.
Each line below shows only the part of the target after the reward, so the one difference stands alone.
Equation 2. A robot that must stay safe while it still explores, and a robot whose practice falls cost nothing, need different targets.
Take a look at this equation. Q-learning aims at the top score, and SARSA aims at the drawn move.

The Q-learning line. Max over a reads the largest score over the moves. It picks the top score among them, not the move itself. Q of the next cell and each move is the score there. Gamma, the discount, is one here, so the next score counts in full. Intuitively, Q-learning aims at the best move next, whatever the robot plays.
termList: Q of the next cell and each move

units.spoken: Intuition. Q-learning aims at the best move next, whatever the robot plays. Its target reads the top score in the next cell.
Example. Take the next cell above the ledge, where the top-scored move runs right along the edge. Q-learning's target reads that top score, whatever move the robot draws.

The SARSA line. Q of the next cell and the drawn move is its score. It reads the drawn move's score, not the top score there. The discount gamma is one here, so the next score counts in full. The two lines differ in one symbol only, the drawn move in place of the top score. Intuitively, SARSA aims at the move it really plays.
termList: Q of the next cell and the drawn move

units.spoken: Intuition. SARSA aims at the move it really plays. Its target reads the score of the drawn move, slips included.
Example. Take the same next cell, where the drawn move steps down toward the ledge. SARSA's target reads the score of that move down, so it carries the fall the robot may take.
Together the two lines say one thing: the drawn move in place of the top score is the whole difference between the two methods.

Here is the point of this figure. Two learners, two sources of teaching. SARSA takes its lessons only from moves its own policy chose, so every lesson comes from a move it really took. Q-learning takes lessons from steps a different policy took as well, the ghost move, a step its own policy did not play. That is why the two methods need different targets: one aims at the move it plays, the other at the best move anywhere.

Figure 6 shows the difference: whose steps teach each learner. SARSA learns only from the steps its own policy plays, while Q-learning also learns from the ghost move, the dashed outline above the row, a step another policy took that its own policy did not play. Take the edge route: a step down toward the ledge, taken by another policy, still teaches Q-learning.

sections.section: 6 The code draws the next move before the update

units.spoken: Section six, The code draws the next move before the update
Gymnasium is the library that supplies the floor: one call builds the cliff walking floor, with its start, ledge and dock.
First the table and the move choice.
This code builds the floor and the table, and sets the four settings.

First, make the floor and an all-zero table with one row per square and one column per move. Second, set the discount, the learning rate, the exploring chance and the episode count, 500. A bigger learning rate moves each score further per step, a bigger discount counts later rewards more, a bigger exploring chance tries more random moves, and more episodes give the tables more chances to settle. Third, rng is the source of the random numbers, seeded with 0 so the run draws the same random moves every time and can be repeated exactly. Fourth, epsilon-greedy picks a random move with chance epsilon, otherwise the move with the top score in the square's row, the move drawn from the epsilon-greedy policy.
Then the loop, with the next move drawn before the update.
This code runs one episode, drawing the next move before each update.

First, each episode starts at the start square and runs until the dock. The terminated flag is true only at the dock. A fall is an ordinary step, so the episode goes on, and Cliff Walking has no step limit, so the truncated flag never ends it. Second, the names r, s next and a next stand for r sub t plus one, s sub t plus one and a sub t plus one, the reward, the next state and the next move. The next move is drawn before the update, so the target reads its score, the surprise measures the gap to the played score, and the update nudges the played score by a share of that surprise. Third, the target is the step's reward alone at the dock, and the step's reward plus the drawn move's score elsewhere; the played score then moves a share of the way toward it.
The loop closes by handing the drawn move over as the move to play.
This code hands the drawn move over as the move to play.
First, the drawn move becomes the move played next, so it is never drawn twice; the loop then runs the same step again from the new cell.
Section seven, Where each learner's route runs

Each robot's route is the path its best moves trace from the start, drawn as arrows in Figure 7. A route counts as reaching the dock only if it gets there without a loop. As exploring rises, SARSA's route moves back from the ledge while Q-learning's stays along the edge, because SARSA's scores beside the ledge carry the fall risk, while Q-learning's best-move scores do not.

The lesson of this figure is that both learners begin with empty tables on one shared floor, and the slider is the experiment. Turn exploring up and the two routes split: SARSA's route moves back from the ledge, because its scores carry the fall risk, while Q-learning's route stays along the edge, because its best-move scores do not. The fall bars tell the same story in numbers: SARSA falls less while it learns.

Try moving the slider to some exploring and pressing Play. Watch the two routes and the fall bars: SARSA's route moves back from the ledge as exploring rises, while Q-learning's stays along the edge, and the fall counts split the same way.

The point of Figure 7 is what the two ends of the slider show. With no exploring, both routes end on the edge, and the falls are only the early ones, before the tables settle. With some exploring, the falls bars give each learner's fall count.

sections.section: 8 Starting scores, the dock step and the settings

units.spoken: Section eight, Starting scores, the dock step and the settings
What the update needs to run
Picture the first update: every score starts at zero, and the step into the dock has no next score to add.
Begin with every score at zero, hopeful because every real score is below zero, so untried moves look best, and let the dock step take the reward alone.
When it works, untried moves get tried because they look best, and the dock step adds nothing extra.
Eight point one, Starting scores and the dock step

On this floor every value is below zero, because every step costs battery. A value is a score. Starting every score at zero is hopeful when every real score is below zero, because moves not yet tried then look best, as taught in Q-Learning.
Only the step that reaches the dock uses the step's reward alone. A fall is an ordinary step.
Eight point two, What each setting does
This table lists the settings this page uses, and what raising or lowering each one does. Find a setting in the first column and read across to see what it changes.
Take the learning rate in Table 1: each update moves the played score part of the gap toward its target. Each step updates one table entry, and the table holds 48 rows by 4 moves.

sections.section: 9 When mistakes while learning cost something

units.spoken: Section nine, When mistakes while learning cost something

SARSA fits where mistakes made while learning cost something real, a robot near a ledge or a live system that can break while it tries random moves. SARSA's route runs along the top row, so the random moves it still takes after training land on safe floor, not the ledge. When only the final route matters and practice falls are free, prefer Q-Learning.

sections.section: 10 Routes that stay too timid or too bold

units.spoken: Section ten, Routes that stay too timid or too bold
Five ways the route goes wrong
Picture the learned route: it can hug the ledge, sit too far from it, or never settle, and each shape points at one mistake.
Read a row of the table across: the cause, the symptom on the floor, and the fix.
When it works, each wrong route names its own fix, and fixing the update fixes the route.
This table lists five ways the route goes wrong, and what helps. Find a cause in the first column and read across to the symptom and the fix.
Take the first row: aiming at the top-scored move instead of the drawn one turns SARSA into Q-learning, and the route hugs the ledge again.
Section eleven, Learning from remembered steps

A table needs a row for every state. Deep Q-Networks swap the table for a neural network and learn from remembered steps. The memory, called replay, holds past steps, and the network trains on those steps again, so a step the robot took long ago can still teach it now. Actor-critic methods also learn from the moves they play: the actor picks each move and the critic judges how good it was, as the Policy Gradient Methods page shows.
